summary: A woman who made a neder not to benefit from people may still take the gifts for the poor. And a neder against Kohanim and Leviim does not stop them from taking their gifts.

chunks.en: "Konam, that I will not benefit from people,"
chunks.st: If a woman vowed: The property of other people is konam for me, and for that reason I will not benefit from it,

chunks.en: he cannot undo it,
chunks.st: her husband cannot nullify

chunks.he: וִיכוֹלָה הִיא לֵהָנוֹת בְּלֶקֶט וּבְשִׁכְחָה וּבְפֵאָה.
chunks.en: and she may benefit from leket, shikchah, and peah.
chunks.st: her vow, but nevertheless, if she is poor, she may benefit from the agricultural gifts that must be left for the poor: Gleanings, i.e., isolated stalks that fell during the harvest; forgotten sheaves; and produce of the corners [pe’a] of the field that the owner is obligated to leave for the poor.
chunks.stMore: Enjoyment of these gifts is not considered as benefit derived from people, as these gifts are not given voluntarily out of the kindness of the donors, but in the performance of a mitzva.

words.note: Stalks dropped in harvest, left for the poor.
Bundles forgotten in the field, left for the poor.
The corner of the field, left for the poor.

chunks.he: קוֹנָם שֶׁאֵינִי עוֹשָׂה עַל פִּי אַבָּא,

chunks.stMore: to receive. If she does more than the fixed amount of work that a woman is obligated to perform for her husband, the vow will be valid with respect to the excess to which he is not entitled, and he might inadvertently come to benefit from something that is forbidden to him.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says,

summary: If a man undid a neder but made a mistake about who made it or what it was about, he must undo it again.

chunks.en: His wife made a neder, and he thought his daughter made it;
chunks.st: If a man’s wife took a vow and he thought that it was his daughter who had taken a vow,

chunks.en: she made a neder to be a nazir, and he thought it was a korban;
chunks.st: or if his wife vowed to be a nazirite and he thought that she had vowed to bring an offering,

chunks.en: she made a neder of a korban, and he thought it was nezirus;

summary: If she made one neder about two things, keeping part keeps all of it. If she made two nedarim, each one is separate.

chunks.he: אָמְרָה, קוֹנָם תְּאֵנִים וַעֲנָבִים אֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵינִי טוֹעֶמֶת,
chunks.en: She said, "Konam, these figs and grapes, that I will not taste,"

chunks.st: these are viewed as two separate vows; if the husband upholds one of the vows it has no effect on the other one.

summary: If a man did not undo a neder because he did not know the halachah, may he undo it when he finds out? Rabbi Meir and the Sages argue.
stIntro: If a man’s wife or daughter took a vow and he failed to nullify the vow on the day he heard it, but afterward he said:

chunks.en: "I knew that there are nedarim,

chunks.en: he may undo it. "I knew that some can undo, but
chunks.st: i.e., he was unaware of the possibility of nullifying vows, he can nullify the vow of his wife or his daughter on the day he learned that he can nullify vows. If, however, he said: I know there are those who can nullify vows, but

chunks.en: I did not know that this is a neder,"
chunks.st: I refrained from nullifying the vow that I heard because I do not know that this is considered a vow,
